newsitem.title: USA: Japan, debt news help Russia at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Japan, debt news help Russia at G7 summit.

text.p: Russia promised on Friday ahead of a Group of Seven summit to stop pointing missiles at Pacific neighbor Japan and won a chance of getting back money lent to Soviet-era allies.

Kremlin officials said Russian President Boris Yeltsin would set up a telephone hotline with Japan and a Japanese spokesman said there would be regular bilateral summits with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said Russia would be admitted to the Paris Club of creditor nations, a group of countries that lend money to debtors like Russia itself.

"I'm very pleased," Clinton told reporters as he met Yeltsin. "What you see here is a sweeping integration of Russia into the major decision-making networks of the world in a way that is very positive for the rest of us."

Russia's full integration into the industrialized world's political and economic institutions had been Yeltsin's main aim at the summit, attended by the leaders of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
Fighting fit again after a long illness, Yeltsin will attend more sessions this year than at any previous G7 summit and he clearly enjoyed the first full day of his Denver visit.
"Denver is good," he told a crowd of around 200 people outside the hotel where he met Clinton. The crowd chanted "Yeltsin, Yeltsin" when he headed towards them to shake some hands.

The Russian president will be excluded from an hour-long session on financial and macro-economic issues -- a reflection of the wide gulf separating Russia from the other states in terms of wealth and economic development.

Frosty ties with Japan have been an obstacle to Russia's ambitions to join the G7 and Tokyo has been reluctant to contemplate a bigger Russian role until a dispute over the status of a group of Pacific islands is resolved.
But the initiatives on a hotline and regular summits, and Moscow's decision to stop aiming its missiles at targets in Japan, clearly put ties on a better footing.
"It is quite a big step," a Japanese official told a news briefing. "Two flows are merging into one flow."
A Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman said remarks by a Japanese official earlier on Friday that Yeltsin promised to stop pointing missiles at China was wrong.
"The official mentioned China by mistake. In the Yeltsin- Hashimoto summit, only Japan was mentioned and there was no mention of China in relation to the missile targets," the spokesman told Reuters.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky also denied that China was mentioned. "There was no discussion of China on this," he said.
Russia has been seeking a bigger global economic role, including membership of the Paris Club, the World Trade Organization and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.
It inherited both the debts and the liabilities of the former Soviet Union, and has won deals to reschedule its multi-billion dollar debts to creditor states and banks.
Yastrzhembsky said Paris Club membership would help Russia recover what he described as $120-140 billion lent by the Soviet Union to its Cold War allies.
"These debts are a heavy burden," he said. "We expect Paris Club membership will help us to start resolving this."
Vietnam and Ethiopia are among big debtors to Moscow.
